utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before the next witness is brought in, I would ask that Mr. Resch and I be excused, and we thank the Court for this opportunity, and counsel as well. And it may also be the case that Ms. Sutherland would welcome the opportunity to enter as we exit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But where is Ms. Sutherland? Ms. Gustin is looking after that. Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Tieger. Thank you, Mr. Resch. The witness is here. Who will be leading -- you will be leading, but who will be cross-examining?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I believe Ms. Sutherland is cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning to you. Can you follow what I am saying in a language that you can understand? Are you receiving interpretation in Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman, we are agreed that this will be in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. You are about to start giving evidence, and before you do so, our Rules require that you enter, you make a solemn declaration, equivalent to an oath, in terms of which you undertake that in the course of your testimony, you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text, I see, has already been handed to you by the usher, so what's left is that you read that out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking, equivalent to an oath. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your name is Boro Mandic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born on 20 February of 1951?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber, if you will, about your educational background. What schools did you attend, what degrees did you receive, where did you go to school? Just a general statement of your educational background.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: I am a lawyer and an economist. I have both degrees. I completed the secondary management school in Zagreb in 1970, after which I found employment, and in parallel with employment, I continued to study law. I got my degree in economics in 1976 and my law degree in 1989, at the Banja Luka university.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your employment during the time that you were studying?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Throughout my university studies of both economics and law, I was employed. I worked all that time in the Municipal Assembly of Celinac from the 1st of July, 1972.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of jobs did you hold for the municipality of Celinac?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: At the Celinac Municipal Assembly I occupied many different positions. Most of the time I spent in verification authorities, inspection authorities, working as a trade inspector, inspector of labour and labour safety, and I also worked as an auditor. For a while I was also heading the audit department. In the 1980s, or more precisely 1983, I was elected secretary of the Municipal Assembly and served for one term of office. After that, I returned to inspection services, where I continued to work until 1988. Correction. 1998. In 1998 I was elected secretary of the Municipal Assembly, in which office I stayed until the first multiparty elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina. As secretary of the Municipal Assembly, I served as secretary of the municipal electoral committee during the first multiparty elections. I did that job well, and on the 19th of December, 1990, I participated as an expert and secretary of the Municipal Assembly in the transition or transfer of duties from the old government to the new government, which won the majority of votes at the multiparty elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The transcript reflects, sir, that you said that you were elected secretary of the Municipal Assembly in 1998, and I think it was 1988 that that happened, was it not?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: 1988. I'm sorry about this. 1988.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did there ever come a time that you had any kind of responsibilities with regard to the Executive Board in Celinac municipality?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, as for my responsibility in the electoral committee, during my first term of office, and at the old government in 1983, in 1984, and under the new government from early January 1990, I occupied that position, as secretary of the electoral committee, I was in charge of administrative affairs and technical affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Sir, we traditionally take a break at 10.30, so you've been here a very short time. I think the Court will want to take a short recess now and we'll get right back to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wasn't expecting Your Honours to go right on before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I explained that I have a meeting with the registrar at 10.30, so stopping earlier would have frustrated that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's no problem. Can I at some stage during today just raise a couple of administrative matters. I will be in Court for the rest of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you prefer immediately after we resume?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to highlight two aspects is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm leaving it to you whether you prefer 25 minutes from now or whether you prefer at the end of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Your Honour why don't we wait until the end of the day if Your Honour gives me five minutes then because in fact that may assist in what I want to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So at the end of the day roughly before --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: About 25 to 2.00. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. So we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My apologies to -- wait for the accused first. My apologies to everyone for going beyond the 25-minute break, but, as I told you before, I had a meeting with the Registrar, which was pretty urgent, and it just lasted a few minutes more than I had hoped it would last. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I think we had gotten through the multiparty elections. I want to ask you: What political party were you a member of at the time of these multiparty elections?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: I would like to tell to the Honourable Chamber, before I answer this question: I don't understand English that well, but it seems to me that I made a mistake when giving one of my previous answers regarding the Executive Board of Celinac municipality. I worked there from 1983 to 1984. That was under the old government. And then I took the new office on the 15th of January, 1991, not 1992. So that was my mistake. So can I please be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That goes on record. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you, then, the question: During the multiparty elections, what political party were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Since I was the secretary of the municipal electoral committee, during the preparations and during the multiparty elections, I was not a member of any of the parties. After the multiparty elections, I did not join any political party, and to this very day I have not belonged to any political party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you've never been a member, for instance, of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: No. I was never an SDS member, nor will I ever be an SDS member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that have any effect upon your positions after the multiparty -- well, let me ask you this question first: In the multiparty elections, who won the majority of the seats in the Celinac Assembly? What party?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: At the first multiparty elections in Celinac, the Serbian Democratic Party won the majority of votes, about 85 per cent. All the other parties shared about 20 per cent of votes between themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a result of the victory of the SDS in that election, was your position affected in any way?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: The position of all those people, regardless of their profession, regardless of their education, that is, all of the people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, depended on the multiparty elections. All the parties in power, the HDZ, the SDA, the SDS, appointed nobody else but members of their respective parties. This obviously reflected on the first composition of the Executive Board in Celinac. When people were appointed to their offices, at the very beginning, I was not given any office, and the same applied to everybody else who didn't belong to that particular party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was a period of time, at least, when you did not have a position because you were not a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: That was the only reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to look at a couple of documents now, just to establish a couple of things. It's DB151 and DB153, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just mention. These are in fact -- obviously I think Mr. Ackerman wants to put them in, but they are already in the Celinac binder, these documents, as Prosecution exhibits, if Your Honour needs to cross-reference them, or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you for that information. Do we have the cross-reference, Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. I only saw these now. They were given to Ms. Sutherland last night and I recognised them as being documents that were already in as Prosecution exhibits. I can check over the next break what the numbers are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Actually, they were given to Ms. Sutherland yesterday morning, not last night. Your Honour, while that comes to mind, I do -- I would -- there's something I would like to place on the record. Yesterday morning -- the day before yesterday, when we met with the witness for the first time, he had brought a -- I think 11 documents with him that, of course, were in B/C/S and not translated. We wanted to use them, and we gave them to CLSS yesterday morning, with some hope that they might be able to translate them in time for us to use them. And they were able to do all of those documents and get them into my hands by 5.30 last night, and I just want to commend publicly, on the record, CLSS for the amazing work that they did to get that done for us and to assist the Defence and this Trial Chamber. They really deserve a lot of credit for that. It was an extraordinary effort that they made. And then just for the record, I then sent them, shortly after I got them to the Prosecutor, by e-mail, so they were delivered to the Prosecution last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman, for that commendation, which I share with you. The work of that section of the Tribunal, as well as of the interpreters, is so heavy, and I think we do well to show our appreciation every now and then the efforts that they make to keep the works of this Tribunal going in an efficient manner. Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So the first document that you have, then, could you just, very briefly, tell the Chamber, this DB151, what this document represents. What is it?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: This document is a decision on the appointment of the president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Celinac, and it says that the Municipal Assembly, on the 19th of December, 1990, appointed Radoslav Brdjanin as president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Celinac. The second document, DB151B, that is, DB153, it says that the Crisis Staff of Celinac municipality, at its session held on the 12th of June, dismisses Radoslav Brdjanin from the position of the president of the Executive Board. So Radoslav Brdjanin is relieved by this decision, and this decision will be ratified by the Assembly of the Celinac municipality at its first coming session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. To your knowledge, then, did Mr. Brdjanin serve as president of the Executive Board in Celinac between the dates of 19 December 1990 and 12 June 1992? In other words, did he serve continuously in that position between those two dates, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: I'm very familiar with the fact that Mr. Brdjanin did hold this position from the date of his appointment to the date of his release. He held regular sessions at -- I participated in all those sessions as the technical secretary of the municipality. I didn't take the minutes, but I did make my own notes, together with the president, I prepared the sessions of the Executive Board, and during that period of time, the Executive Board worked in its full composition, and I must say that it worked very correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was it, being a non-member of the SDS, that you were able to secure this position of secretary, then, with the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you how this happened. The Executive Board, at its very beginning, was composed mostly of the members of the Serbian Democratic Party, although I must say before this Trial Chamber that Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin did not agree with that. He insisted on the Executive Board to consist of experts in their respective fields, regardless of their party affiliation, regardless of their religious affiliation or ethnical background. And very soon after that, probably against a lot of opposition in his party, he managed to succeed in changing the composition of the Executive Board so that from then on, members of the Executive Board were also people who were not members [Realtime transcript read in error "in the members"] of the SDS. I was a technical secretary. I did not vote. I did not make any decisions. However, other members who participated in the very important work of the Executive Board were people who were never members of the SDS, before that or after that. For example, Nenad Joldzic was the secretary for economy and the Vice-President for the Executive Board and he was appointed on the insistence of Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin. Mr. Vlado Vrhovac was the director of the revenue administration. Then Nemanja Bilanovic, who was also a lawyer and who was born in a mixed marriage, he was a misdemeanour judge in that term of office. His position was very important. Later on, he became a member of the Executive Board, as the director of cadastral services. Very soon after that, people were appointed to some professional duties who, before the change of power, were not assigned to any duties. One of them was Vitomir Djuric, another one was Borislav Gavric. The point that I'm making here is that very soon the Executive Board was led by the Executive Board -- the Executive Board was led by Mr. Brdjanin, although its members were not all of them members of the party in power.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the transcript, page 40, line 13, it says: "Members of the Executive Board were also people who were in the members of the SDS." What the members witness said was who were not members of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you okay with that, Ms. Sutherland or Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's my recollection too. All right. So that goes on record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber when you first met Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: I first met Mr. Brdjanin when we were still very young. The first time I got to know him was in primary school. He's three years older than me, and he was in the fourth grade while I was in the first grade. Then I changed schools because in that place, the school went up to the fourth grade only. So I went to school in Kotor Varos, whereas Mr. Brdjanin continued his education in Celinac. Later on, I continued my education in Zagreb, and Mr. Brdjanin went to Banja Luka and Novi Sad. We went to university in different places, so that we didn't see each other for a long time. It was only in the '80s when I saw him again, when Mr. Brdjanin became the director of a large construction company in Celinac, and by that time I had already worked in the Municipal Assembly for quite a number of years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You worked with Mr. Brdjanin when you were secretary of the Executive Board, and as the Chamber will learn, later, as he became a minister. The question I want to ask you was: Did you at any time become close friends with Mr. Brdjanin? When I say "close friends," I mean social friends who would visit each other's homes and things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: I'll be very honest. Although we lived in a very small place, that is to say, Mr. Brdjanin lived in Banja Luka and worked in Celinac, and I myself lived in Celinac - I was never close friends with him. We only had a professional relationship. That is only as of lately. I was never in his house, I was never in his apartment in Banja Luka, nor was he ever in my house. And since none of us patroned bars and pubs, we never actually met in any of those either. So to cut this long story short, we met in the Executive Board and our relationship was strictly professional.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that period of time immediately following the multiparty elections, and specifically, beginning 19 December 1990 through 12 June 1992, when Mr. Brdjanin served as president of the Executive Board, what was the approximate percentage of non-Serb inhabitants of the Celinac municipality, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: The last census was carried out in 1990. According to that census, about 95 per cent of the population of Celinac were Serbs. Only 5 per cent, or thereabouts, were Muslim, Bosniaks, or others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the municipality of Celinac during this same period of time that we're talking about, 19 December 1990 to 12 June 1992, were there non-Serb persons employed in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: There were non-Serbs in the municipality. Before the multiparty elections, as well as after the multiparty elections. I know it very well because I gave a number of them their jobs. Because up to the first multiparty elections, I had worked in the municipality for some 17 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ackerman, because I want to have this clear in my mind. Could I ask Ms. Gustin to help me here. There is a document which gives us the figure of the 1990 census. Because I'm sure that we either have a mistake in the interpretation. Because he says that the last census was carried out in 1990 and then 95 per cent of the population of Celinac was Serbs. Is that correct? Because I think it was much more mixed than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Exhibit P1150 is the 1991 census, Your Honour. I thought it was P60. That's what I said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P60. If we can have a look at P60, please. Sorry, Mr. Ackerman, about this, but I think ... So it seems that in the 1991, 1991, there doesn't seem to have been a census in 1990, in any case. But in 1991, the percentage of Croats --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That the percentage of Croats was significant, 0.4. The percentage of Muslims was 7.7. The percentage of Serbs was 88.5. And then Yugoslavs and others, we have 2 per cent and 1.4 per cent. So it's a little bit different from the 95 that you mentioned. Anyway, just for the record, were you referring to some other more recent census? Is it a census that was held after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I think that the first census after the war -- I can comment on that, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem. The important thing is that we have clarified this, because I was aware that we had never heard of a census in 1990, to start with. And I wanted to clear this up so that at least, you know -- so it's not important. Let's go ahead. If you need to say anything about it, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to make myself clear. You must know that I have no statistical records in front of me. I'm just speaking from my memory. I know that we always had 5 per cent of Muslim population, and a part of the Serb population declared themselves as Yugoslavs, which reduced the percentage of declared Serbs. But the figure that sticks in my mind is around 95 per cent of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question I want to ask you now is: Did the number of non-Serbs working in the municipality come anywhere near matching the census figures, whatever those are? Was it a 5 to 7 per cent of non-Serbs who worked in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: First of all, we had very solid and stable legislation and regulations on employment, which did not insist on reflecting the ethnic composition in employment. But since I had worked there for a long time, I am aware that we had 6 to 7 employees of other ethnicities out of the total of 90, or around 90.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over the years - and I'm mostly interested in 1991, 1992, when you were working with Mr. Brdjanin - during that period of time, did you have an opportunity to observe or learn what his attitude was toward non-Serb people? For instance, did he make efforts to get the non-Serb people working for the Celinac municipality dismissed, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: I must say to the Honourable Trial Chamber that with the transition of government and the takeover of duties in the municipality by Mr. Brdjanin, none of the employees, Serb or otherwise, were dismissed. Therefore, throughout 1990, all the employees continued in their jobs, as before the multiparty elections. For instance, there are very important positions that were manned by Muslims. When the war began in 1991, the mobilisation of soldiers into the Army of Republika Srpska was handled in the military department by a man who was a Muslim. In the staff of National Defence, a very important position was held by a Muslim. Head of accounting was also a Muslim, that is, a Bosniak. Our misdemeanour judge came from a mixed marriage. The secretary of Mr. Brdjanin was a Croat lady or, more precisely, a Polish woman of Roman Catholic faith. Mr. Brdjanin's driver was a Muslim. I will not enumerate any more, but from the head of accounting to the secretary in the town hall, many non-Serbs continued to work throughout the war in these positions, and even afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, line -- page 45, line 10, the witness said 1991, instead of 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you okay with that, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't recall. The witness then goes on in the next sentence: When the war began in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's the next sentence, however. We have on record here that you said: Therefore, throughout 1990, all the employees continued in their jobs, as before the multiparty elections. Did you mean -- did you say 1990, throughout 1990, or throughout 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Throughout 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Starting with the multiparty elections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought so. All right, would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Otherwise it wouldn't have made any sense, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your position as secretary to the Executive Board in Celinac, what were your duties? What kind of things did you do?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: I think it is widely known what the technical secretary of a body --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Ackerman, if you are interested in one or more functions rather than all the others, you are free to put a very direct question to the witness. And because otherwise we will probably hear a whole description of functions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me then do some background before I then ask you the question the Judge suggests. After you left the Celinac Executive Board, just very briefly tell us what positions you have held since your position with the Executive Board in Celinac. What other positions have you held and what are you doing now?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: I occupy the position of the secretary of the Executive Board until November 1992. I was then appointed assistant minister for legal and economic affairs in the ministry for construction of Republika Srpska. This position I continue to occupy today. In those 12 years that I have worked in the government of Republika Srpska, the most years, or the most terms of office, or the most governments, I was assistant minister. During Dodik's term, I was assistant minister, and in the new composition of the Assembly, I am assistant for legal and administrative affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When we go -- we go back now, then, to the Celinac Executive Board. When that board arrived at various decisions and conclusions, was it your job to prepare those and issue them?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Sometimes, but mostly not. The Executive Board operates in the following way. They get ready-made, prepared materials from proposing agencies, from the municipality, with the ready-made proposal for a conclusion or a decision. If the Executive Board accepts that draft or proposal without any changes, the president signs it and the technical service of the Executive Board delivers their decision to receiving agencies. If some changes are made, then the president gets it for signature, and only then does the technical service pass it on to the so-called users.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the things that we have seen through this trial is that documents coming from various boards, assemblies, staffs, have different names. Some of them are called conclusions, some of them are called decisions. In the course of your legal training and your experience dealing with these kinds of documents, do you know the difference between, for instance, a conclusion and a decision?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: I know that very well. The Executive Board most of the time adopted conclusions. Sometimes decisions and determinations. All of them are enactments, legally speaking. The Executive Board rarely made decisions, because in the hierarchy of legal enactments, it is a higher act, a higher enactment. Therefore, the Executive Board made conclusions based on background materials that were considered by the Executive Board. So let me repeat. In most of the cases, in the majority of cases, the Executive Board adopted the conclusions, whose nature was rather organisational and operational, or operative, than legal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is a conclusion, then, is not necessarily a binding document of any kind, but more, say, advisory? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, most of the time those are advisory conclusions, invitations to cooperation, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who decides whether a document is going to be called a decision or a conclusion? Who makes that decision?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: That decision is made by the proposing agency, in compliance with the law. For instance, if a municipal agency proposes an expropriation of land to be effected, then they propose a document called a determination, and it cannot be otherwise. It is established practice, as a matter of law. If something is to be adopted, then the proposing agency suggests that it be made in the form of a conclusion. And if something has really to be decided, and that was rare, then it was to be a decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We were talking a few moments ago about Mr. Brdjanin's attitude toward non-Serb people in the Celinac municipality. I want to show you a document. It is P1998, that was issued by the War Presidency in Celinac after Mr. Brdjanin had left. And I want to ask you if you're familiar with this document, and what, if anything, you know about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one moment. Can we go into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And the question is?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document, and what do you have to tell us about it, if anything?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: In the statement I gave previously, in my earlier testimony, in fact, I said I worked as an expert in the Executive Board. The Executive Board is in no way related to the War Presidency. I never laid eyes on this decision before, nor have I ever heard about it, although it was talked about after the war. To be precise, in some recent contacts I had, I learned that a decision of this sort existed. However, I never worked in the War Presidency, and I have absolutely no information about their dealings, so I cannot comment on this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had indicated that following the multiparty elections, when Mr. Brdjanin wanted to staff the Executive Board with non-SDS members, I think the language you used was that you understood he had some difficulty about that, or some problems with the SDS about that. Is that true? Do you know that he had difficulties when he tried to staff the Executive Board with non-SDS people?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. But I have to say right away that I have no data in front of me, but I speak from my own knowledge. It is the only municipality in all of Bosnia and Herzegovina where there was one ruling party, and the Executive Board still included non-members of that ruling party. I do not know whether Mr. Brdjanin had any problems because of this within his party, but I hold the opinion - and that opinion is based on what I occasionally heard - that he was sometimes reprimanded for the fact that he surrounded himself with people who do not belong to the party, being president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this decision we were just looking at from the War Presidency, do you know, first of all, if this was a decision made by persons who were members of the SDS party; and second, would you say that Mr. Brdjanin would have agreed with a decision like this?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't know who was on the War Presidency. I don't know whether all the members were also members of the Serbian Democratic Party. I believe that some non-members of SDS were on the Presidency as well. But from Article 2, which I'm looking at right now, for the first time, I must say, I think that if we asked Mr. Brdjanin -- in fact, if he had had a say, he would never have accepted this, because some of these people are friends of Mr. Brdjanin, and his neighbours. Most of them were employed in his enterprise. And if it had been his decision, he would not have phrased it this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the Sugic brothers?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear about what they were doing in the Celinac municipality?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to tell you frankly that there are many things that passed me by, because there was a war going on. I didn't like it. I didn't want it. I didn't ask for it. And I tried to keep away from it as much as I could. However, certain things you couldn't help hearing. So I heard that, allegedly, the Sugic brothers, after the killing of one of them, set an ambush and killed some people. I don't know whether it was really the Sugic brothers who did it. I have no way of knowing. What I know is that Mr. Brdjanin, and some other people in positions of responsibility, condemned this act. And Mr. Brdjanin condemned it particularly strongly. And as far as I know, these brothers were then arrested, kept in detention, and later released, only to be detained again. And for all I know, they found themselves in detention again. After the war they were arrested, and I think they are still in prison today. I think they had stood trial at some point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you recall an incident in Celinac, I think perhaps in August of 1992, involving a large number of Muslim citizens being placed on buses. Do you recall anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: That day is very clearly etched in my memory. It was by far the most difficult day of my life, and for that reason I kindly ask this Honourable Court to let me speak about this event. Because it must have been planned, but, thank heaven, it ended well. I believe it happened in the beginning of August. I worked in the municipality at that time, and all of us who were at work that day had occasion to see that that day, in the morning, several buses filled with people arrived outside the town hall. I don't know how many buses exactly there were, because I could see only two or three of them from my window. People were talking and saying that those people on the buses were those who had expressed their wish to go somewhere, to Travnik, for instance, and that transport had been organised for them. In the meantime, these people were filing into the buses, and then out of them, until eventually news travelled through our building like a flash, that the building of the municipality is surrounded, under blockade, and that no one is allowed to leave. I personally, and everyone around me, could see that downstairs, at the intersection, and on the bridge, there were people in uniforms, soldiers, very tall men in black clothing, black hats, wearing automatic weapons, intercepting people, stopping them, abusing them. And very soon, people stopped leaving their homes. All of this continued throughout the day. Sometime around 5.00 p.m., these soldiers who had arrived from outside of our locality, because none of the locals that I spoke to knew them. So after 5.00 p.m., these people dispersed, because our regular police, and the military police, which was also referred as the corps police from Banja Luka, came, dispersed this gang, ran them out of town. And then around 6.00 p.m., I noticed that the buses I had seen earlier were moved to the school building. The people were given food and drink, and military security was provided. They stayed there for two or three days, until the situation calmed down, and the people returned to their homes. I want to make a point of mentioning that the next day, when I came to work --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you just a minute. Who were the people that were on the buses? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: The people on the buses were all Muslims. A lot of them I knew personally, because they were our neighbours, ordinary people, most of them correct people. And that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people in the black uniforms, did you ever find out who they were?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: No. I couldn't really see them too well. I couldn't recognise them. Later on we all heard that those were -- some people who came from outside. They were not members of the Army of Republika Srpska. They were not members of a renegade government. Most people assumed - and I suppose they were correct - that those people came from somewhere outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Brdjanin have anything to do with that incident? Did he play any role in it at all?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: On that day when we were being held captives in the municipal building, Mr. Brdjanin was not in Celinac. Later on I heard - that was on the following day - that Mr. Brdjanin, as a representative of the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska, used his authority as a representative and as a humanitarian, he used his authority in favour of the Muslim population of Celinac municipality and asked the police to intervene on their behalf and disperse this unwelcome gang, and for these Muslims to be placed somewhere safe. It is very important to say at this point that in the entire area of Celinac municipality, news spread at the time that these unknown persons had set up mortar nests between Celinac and Banja Luka, and if that convoy had set on its way, I believe that the worst thing would have happened to them. All the citizens of Celinac know that the lives of the people on those buses were saved by Mr. Brdjanin, who prevented a tragedy because he respected his fellow citizens of Celinac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say there was this roadblock set up, was that the same people in the black uniforms and you believe that they intended to massacre these people? Is that what you're saying to this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: This is what I wanted to say, but because all those who saw the incident told the same story, and the story spread much more on the following day. On that day, there was very little said, because everybody feared everybody else, and nobody knew exactly what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people, then, that were placed in the school, and I think you said that there were guards at the school then, were they being held prisoner there or were they being protected there? Which?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't know, because I wasn't there. I was at home. After this unpleasant incident, when I could leave the building, they were in the school. They were absolutely free and protected by the government organs and the regular police. And within the next two or three days, they could move freely about. They would also come to the town hall. I could give you the names of the people who came to see me. Some of them were my friends and acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this period of time that Mr. Brdjanin was president of the Executive Board in Celinac, was Celinac a safe place for non-Muslim people to live -- or non-Serb people to live?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: I believe that during that period of time, in Celinac, as a town neighbourhood, it was safe. And this is where certain people who had come from elsewhere found shelter. Some of them came from Kotor Varos, others came from the neighbouring villages belonging to the Celinac municipality, where there had been incidents. Celinac, as such, was a safe nucleus which stayed that way until the very end of the war, without any major incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to change subjects now. I want you to look now at a document, P323. And mostly I'm interested in decision number 737. This is a document which appoints Mr. Brdjanin minister of the Republika Srpska Ministry of Construction, Spatial Planning, and Transport; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: That's correct. This decision was still being kept at the ministry where I still work, and this is the decision on the appointment of the first minister of construction, spatial planning, and transport. Mr. Brdjanin was appointed to this office on the 15th of September, 1992, and he remained in that position, as far as I can remember, until the 8th of March, 1995, when he was relieved of his duties at his own request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've maybe almost, at least, answered the next question I wanted to ask you. This ministry had not existed prior to Mr. Brdjanin's appointment; is that what you told us?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think it existed. It was established by the government of Republika Srpska, and then people were appointed to various positions. So I believe that it didn't exist before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this ministry located in Pale, along with the rest of the Republika Srpska government, or did it have a different location?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: No. This ministry was in Banja Luka, at the same location where it still exists today. Owing to Mr. Brdjanin, who deserves credit for that. And this is the only ministry that was not in Pale, but rather had its seat in Banja Luka. And as people like to say, it is the first step towards moving the government and all the other ministers to Banja Luka after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that this was the beginning of this ministry, that it had not existed prior to this date, and that -- when did you -- my first question, then, is: When did you become part of this ministry? When were you employed in this ministry?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: I became assistant for legal and economic affairs, and I still hold the same position. I first joined on 19 November 1992, and that was when all the other assistants were appointed in the ministry and when the assistant -- deputy minister was appointed. We were all appointed either on the same day or at least within the space of one month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people who were appointed to that ministry, did Mr. Brdjanin choose SDS members other -- were you the only non-SDS member or were other people also non-SDS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First of all, let's see whether at the time he was still a non-SDS member.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He's already testified that he never was a member of SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were still a non-member of the SDS at the time; no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking me, sir? No, never. Not then, not after that, not ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other people who were appointed to positions in that ministry by Mr. Brdjanin, were they all SDS members, or not?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, as I've already told you: The way Mr. Brdjanin behaved in Celinac when he appointed members to the Executive Board who were non-members of the SDS, he continued behaving the same way, and he formed his inner team, choosing five of his assistants, his deputy, and the chief state inspector. All these people who were chosen, none of them belonged to the SDS. No other cabinet minister of Republika Srpska did that. And I'm almost sure that this was not done either by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the former Yugoslavia. Mr. Brdjanin appointed Borko Djuric as his deputy. He was also not an SDS member. He appointed me, Boro Mandic. He appointed Miladin Gacanovic and Predrag Milosevic. None of us were members of the SDS. He also appointed Predrag Marjanovic, as the main spatial planning inspector. He also was not a member of the SDS. He had just one goal in mind: To appoint people from the profession. Because he believed in professionalism. And this proved to be correct. All of us who were appointed by Mr. Brdjanin continued to hold similar, same, or even higher positions in the government. So he made a good choice, and we met the requirements of every subsequent government. To this very day, I'm still an assistant in the Ministry of Construction, and my minister is a Bosniak, a member of the SDA. Owing to a good selection made by Mr. Brdjanin during his first term of office and a good evaluation of all the other ministers, the Ministry of Construction is one of the best-organised and one of the most efficient ministries in the government of Republika Srpska. A little while ago I spoke at an international conference about the ministry of construction of Republika Srpska, and I said that by the level of our professional qualifications, we are the best in the world. We have four or five people who hold Ph.D.s. We have two or three with just secondary degree. All the rest of us have either one or two full bachelor's degrees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there other people still with the ministry that were appointed by Mr. Brdjanin? Are you the only one, or are there others that are still there?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: No. No. In the ministry, Mr. Miladin Gacanovic, who is an engineer and who is an assistant minister for residential affairs, is still there. One gentleman who used to be an assistant now holds a tenure at the university. The former deputy is now the director of the largest construction company in Republika Srpska. And Mr. Predrag Marjanovic is now retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us a great deal now about -- and given us some examples of Mr. Brdjanin attitude against -- with regard to persons who were not members of SDS. I want you to look at a document, P254. While they're finding the document, just keep in mind what you've told us about Mr. Brdjanin's attitude also toward non-Serb persons.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: When it came to employment and recruiting, all the others who were in high positions in the ministry - lawyer, engineers, accountants - Mr. Brdjanin insisted and looked for those who showed professional qualities. So that people who were employed, unlike in other areas, were women whose husbands were of different ethnic backgrounds, whereas such cases would be punished in other areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Look at this document. It's a document issued by the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina on 22 June 1992, while Brdjanin was president of that crisis staff. In the context of what you've been telling the Chamber, how can you explain this document? It seems to say the opposite.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: I have never seen this document, and I was never close to any crisis staffs, either to the Crisis Staff of Krajina or the Crisis Staff of Celinac. And what it says here is absolutely opposite to what was happening in the Executive Board of Celinac municipality and in the ministry. Whenever Mr. Brdjanin and documentation proves that, and also there are people who can testify to that, because they still work there or are around - whenever Mr. Brdjanin had an opportunity to decide on these matters, like he did in the ministry and in the Executive Board, then he would decide something completely different than transpires from this decision. I don't want to, and I simply can't, interpret this very illegible piece of writing. However, as a lawyer by profession, I know that sometimes a chairperson will sign a decision which is a product of a joint work. If this was issued by the Crisis Staff of the so-called AR Krajina, then I suppose this was the product of a joint work and of the voting on this decision. And in a number of cases, we have seen these things happening, in our respective workplaces, when we had to sign similar decisions. This decision never had its implications, never had any bearing on the ministry where Mr. Brdjanin worked or on the Executive Board of Celinac municipality. Whether this decision was implemented elsewhere, I wouldn't be able to tell you. I only repeat: I have never had any contacts with any crisis staffs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we go back now to the ministry where Mr. Brdjanin appointed all of these people that were not members of the SDS. Do you know if he had any -- that if he was criticised in any way by the authorities in Pale for not employing SDS members in his ministry? Do you know if he had any difficulty about that?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I didn't have frequent contacts with Minister Brdjanin. However, my personal opinion is that he must have been criticised. It only makes sense, in a multiparty system. I believe that Mr. Brdjanin was able to fight back and to do what he did, and I think that he did right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This ministry for construction and so forth, among its responsibilities, was one of those housing?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that the ministry was formed in September, that you and most of the staff came on board in November. When was it the ministry actually was able to get completely organised and start functioning and performing its duties and tasks?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: I know it very well. As an assistant minister, I was in charge of that organisation, and we started working on the 15th of March, 1993, and that was when all of the other positions were filled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of matters were within the ministry's competence with regard to housing? What kind of things did the ministry do with regard to housing?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: The ministry dealt with complaints which came from appellants who appealed against the first-instance decisions made by municipal organs. The ministry mostly decided on the exchange of property or the exchange of tenants' rights between the holders of those rights. From the end of 1993 onwards, it also dealt with the rationalisation of residential space. According to the former law which was passed a long time ago in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina, in 1984, I think it was, every holder of tenants' rights had the right to exchange his rights with another holder of tenants' rights in the territory of the entire former Yugoslavia. This law was still in effect in 1993 and some of its provisions are still in effect. For example, if somebody, for example, a Croat or a Muslim, wanted to exchange their flat with a Serb from Zagreb or from Belgrade, they had to first ask for the consent of the owner of that apartment. That would usually be a company or an enterprise. In most of these cases, the company didn't agree to give their consent. Then the person could appeal with the municipality, and then the municipality acted instead of that company and applied the law and allowed for the apartments to be exchanged. In most cases, municipalities did not allow this to take place, because they probably wanted to give the abandoned flats to the refugees who arrived from Croatia and from the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I remember very well - and there are a number of decisions in our ministry testifying to that - when we started working on the 15th of March, 1993, and when we started dealing with those appeals, Minister Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Brdjanin gathered all the responsible persons around himself and told them: I demand from you to respect the law, to observe the law. This is a state with the rule of law. Everybody has the right to exercise their rights, in keeping with the law. Then our services started to approve exchange of property to all those who were entitled to have their property exchanged. For example, a Croat who wanted to exchange his apartment would come to the ministry, he would pack his things, he would go to Croatia, he would enter another apartment there and continue living freely until the end of the war. This was a very positive development, and this was recognised by the High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina, who after the war passed a law according to which, if somebody regretted their previous decisions, they could go back to their former apartment. And there are such cases. For example, if people subsequently were not satisfied with the decision they made, they could restore their tenancy right in Republika Srpska and return to their former apartment. But most of the decisions made at that time are valid to this very day. Can I please continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We need to have a break here for 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 63, line 24 of the transcript says: A number of decisions. And I'm told what the witness said was: "There are hundreds of decisions in our ministry." So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You want "a hundred" instead of "a number"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What he said was: "There are hundreds of decision," instead of "a number."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you agree to that, sir? I think we had better read out to him. Sir, I'm going to read from the transcript that I have right here in front of me, and then you've heard what Mr. Ackerman said, and you tell me whether you want -- what you want to have on record. "In most cases municipalities did not allow this to take place because they probably wanted to give the abandoned flats to the refugees who arrived from Croatia and from the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I remember very well, and there are a number of decisions --" This is where Mr. Ackerman said you said there are hundreds of decisions. "There are number of decisions and our ministry testifying to that when we started working on the 15th of March, 1993 and when we started dealing with those appeals, Minister Brdjanin," et cetera. Did you see there were a number of such decisions or hundreds of such decisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can say with absolute certainty that there are hundreds, certainly more than 100, and probably hundreds, but not decisions; determinations. The ministry makes determinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the process of making those determinations, did Mr. Brdjanin make distinction between members of different ethnic groups? Did he treat members of different ethnic groups differently?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: No. On the contrary; every decision that had to do with a swap of apartments or the rationalisation of housing space had two opposing parties involved. One of the parties was always a non-Serb. Mr. Brdjanin insisted that we go by the book, that is, by the law, and the law required us to approve the exchange of apartments or rationalisation of housing space, and we did that. It was always signed by Mr. Brdjanin or one of his deputies, and all of these determinations were confirmed by the Supreme Court. In the event that the party who was not satisfied, instituted proceedings, or started a lawsuit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want you to look at some documents. I'm going to ask the Registrar to give you a series of documents, DB154 through DB159, and DB166 through DB169. You can have all those at once and we'll just go through them as quickly as we can. Sir, find DB154, which is the first one I want you to look at.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Here in front of us we see a determination dated the 22nd of March, 1993. That is only seven days after we started working. This is an example of precisely what I was trying to explain. A person of Croat ethnicity, Viktor Skarija, if I need to mention it, asked the owner of the apartment for approval, which was refused, and then from the relevant agency in the municipality, which was also refused, for exchanging an apartment with another person residing in Sisak. So the ministry made this determination, in keeping with the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the determination of the ministry?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: The determination of the ministry reads that the appeal is denied, and the appeal was made by the owner of the apartment, the owner being Cajevic [phoen] company. I remember this enactment very well. The owner of the apartment appealed against the ministry to the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court denied his appeal, which means that the decision initially made by the ministry was lawful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the ministry basically said that the exchange must be allowed?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Look at DB155.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is another example of what I just said. Roda Cajevic, owner of this apartment, unhappy with our decision, that is, the decision of the ministry, appeals against our ministry to the Supreme Court, starting proceedings, and the Supreme Court rejects this appeal as ungrounded in law, which means that the ministry had done its job, in keeping with the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the decision of the ministry to approve the exchange was upheld by the Supreme Court, then?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at 156 now and tell the Chamber what that is.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: This is another example of the same situation that we discussed before. Andrija Anurijven [phoen], a person of Croat ethnicity, is asking for approval to exchange his apartment. He is rejected. And Autoprjevoz company, the owner of the apartment, appealed. The ministry denied his appeal. And as far as I remember, this again reached the Supreme Court, which again confirmed the initial decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you look at, then, the next document, is DB157. Tell us what that document is.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: You must know that I haven't seen all these determinations before, because I didn't deal with them. It was the legal department that was in charge. This determination, again, refers to a case where an exchange of apartments was applied for by Bakir Filipovic, a Muslim. The owner denied his application. The ministry took it under consideration, rescinded the decision of the municipality and returned this case to the municipality, giving clear instructions to the municipality to approve this exchange. The administrative organs of Republika Srpska, and indeed of the entire Yugoslavia, allow for a procedure wherein a decision is first returned to the body that made it, so that the decision is amended. And sometimes it returns it even to the first-instance body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this particular decision, just for instance, involves a Muslim resident of Banja Luka with an apartment in Banja Luka that he wants to exchange --

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That he wants to exchange with somebody in Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Exactly. He wanted to swap apartments with Milan Adzic from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now look at DB158, please, and tell the Judges what that is.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: That is another example of what I tried to explain from memory. When we dealt at the ministry with application for an approval for an exchange of apartment of Andrija Mrvelj, and in this case the Supreme Court denied the appeal made by Autoprjevoz company and proclaimed the ministry's decision as correct and lawful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next is DB159.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: This is another determination, as far as I can see, where the lower body, Banja Luka municipality, instructed, that is, ordered, this Muslim citizen, Fatima Begic, to move out of her apartment within three days and turn over the apartment to the rightful owner. However, the ministry took this appeal of Fatima Begic under consideration, rescinded the decision made before, and decided differently, in conformity with the law, in favour of Fatima Begic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was in December of 1994 that the ministry is ordering that this person --

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Be permitted to remain in the apartment in Banja Luka; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look now at DB166.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: This one is very particular, and I must say a very nice decision. In one previous decision, we, that is, the ministry, rescinded the decision of Banja Luka municipality and instructed the municipality to decide again in favour of Bakir Milic. In renewed proceedings, a negative decision was again made. He appealed to the Ministry of Construction, and the ministry decided on merits, which was a rare occasion. The ministry always -- almost always decided in favour of returning the case to the lower body for adjustment and amendment, but in this case the ministry actually changed the decision itself and decided on merit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go, then, to DB167. I think it's the same case, now in the Supreme Court, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Again, this decision again confirms that the ministry decided correctly. The lawsuit was not won by the appealing party, and the ministry won this lawsuit concerning this decision made in favour of Bakir Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want you to look now at DB169 first, and then we'll go back to 168. DB169 is dated January 29, 1993. It appears to be a letter from Mr. Brdjanin to the president of the IO of Banja Luka, referring to a Mr. Enes Seferagic and regarding an apartment of his mother; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. We have here a case of decision made through correspondence between the ministry, on the one hand - this is signed by Minister Brdjanin, and he's requiring the person in charge in Banja Luka municipality to prevent or stop the eviction of Mrs. Rasida Seferagic, mother of Enes Seferagic who appealed. In this case, no appeal reached the ministry. It was just a complaint lodged with the minister, or it was verbally expressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Could somebody like that just come to the ministry and say: I have a problem I want to talk to Mr. Brdjanin about? Could that happen?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, and I am a witness to that. All assistants from the ministry still keep their agendas to this day. There was no day, no one day at the ministry for receiving citizens. Citizens were always received. In case the minister was there himself, he would receive the citizen or have his assistants receive them. And in the absence of the minister, assistant ministers were always ready to receive the citizens, hear their complaints, and decide, and held the resolution of their cases. There are hundreds of such cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of this document of January 29, 1993, Mr. Brdjanin, after having set out some facts, says: I hope you will issue a positive ruling, and I therefore thank you in advance. Would you look now at DB168, which is in February of 1993, about two weeks later, and apparently --

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. After --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... What the municipality of Banja Luka decided after receiving Mr. Brdjanin's letter.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: This is really the first time I'm looking at this, but I can understand what I read. After this letter, Banja Luka municipality and the responsible agency adopted the conclusion terminating the proceedings instituted ex officio for the eviction of Rasida Seferagic. Therefore, we can see that the lawful intervention of the minister worked, and Mrs. Rasida managed to exercise her right and stay in her apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you arrived here in The Hague, you brought with you a number of documents that you shared with us upon your arrival, and these have now been translated, and they are marked as exhibits DB170 through DB180. And I think we can just go through those one at a time and have you explain to the Trial Chamber the significance of the document. First of all, tell the Trial Chamber where these documents came from.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: These documents come from the ministry's archives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you brought them from the archives, you brought the originals from the archives, and I think those have now been returned to you, so you can return them to the archives. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: They have not been returned yet, but I insist on their recovery. They are not perhaps the most important documents in the world, but they are relevant to this process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I promise you that we'll get them back in your hands before you leave town.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that's happening, I don't know whether Mr. Ackerman thinks he's going to finish today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If not, I wonder if we could stop at half past 1.00, because I realise there are quite a number of matters I need to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. There isn't much left on the basis of the witness summary. I think there are just three or four points left, following your line of questioning. But it's up to him. I'm not going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, we're nearly finished, Your Honour. If we weren't going to stop, we would finish by 1.45, I think. But Ms. Korner does need some time to address you, so I think we probably won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll go through these documents. Do you think we can go through them in five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Probably not. We'll do the best we can. Some of them require some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long do you anticipate the cross-examination to last, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's one of the matters I want to raise, about estimates of cross-examination. I don't think that it will be much more than the two hours that Ms. Sutherland estimated yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's use these five minutes. I mean, I don't fancy wasting them, in any case. So you can start, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let's start with DB170.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are letters. They vary from case to case, but they have similarities. On the 22nd February 1994, Minister Brdjanin received a citizen by the name of Atif Fatkic from Banja Luka, who was asking the footwear factory to resolve her case because the factory had instituted proceedings to move her out of her apartment. This person, Atif Fatkic, who had a disabled son and a wife who was unfit for employment, wanted to stay in his apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what ethnicity is Atif Fatkic?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: Atif is of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does the letter -- what did Mr. Brdjanin say in the letter to the Bosna footwear factory?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: In this letter addressed to the footwear factory, it is noted that Atif Fatkic from Banja Luka appealed to the ministry, against the motion to evict him from his apartment, and the minister wrote a very long letter, saying that disabled persons are involved, and in view of the fact that the procedure for housing rationalisation had not been observed, he is asking that this family be left alone, briefly. That is the gist of the letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at DB171 now, please.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC
utterances.text: In this case, we see a similar situation. Alojz Pilic, I think this is a Croat, was moved by his employer to a different apartment, or was simply evicted, and his apartment was allocated to another person, Vitomir Misic [phoen]. In this case, Mr. Brdjanin, that is, the ministry, demands from the factory, as the owner of the apartment, to follow the procedure, and he says here simply that the previous tenant should be returned to his apartment because his tenancy right is completely legal. In this way, this case is similar to the previous one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think probably we should stop there and allow Ms. Korner to tell you whatever she wants to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So, Mr. Mandic, we need to stop here today because we have got some other business to deal with before our time is over. You will be accompanied by the usher out of this courtroom, and you will return again tomorrow morning, 9.00. We recommence with your testimony, and I'm sure we'll finish with you tomorrow morning. I thank you. Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first matter is one that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's all right, yes. What Your Honour referred to a moment ago, the estimate of cross-examination. We of course base our estimates on the summaries. If a witness comes and says a great deal more that is not concerned -- sorry - not referred to in the summary, then the estimates are not going to be worth very much. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll do our best. And as I say, at the moment this witness appears to be sticking to the summary and I don't think it will be much more than two hours. However, Your Honour, Your Honour ordered, at the Status Conference, or pre-defence conference, on the -- I'll just get the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 9th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 9th, on page 20832 of the transcript that there should be a provisional exhibit list given to us by the 20th of October. And by that, Your Honour, I have no doubt was referring to the rule, which is the exhibits that are intended to be used in the Defence case, not per witness. Your Honour, yesterday we were given -- I don't know if Your Honours got it - Exhibit list submission number 1. That one page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is -- yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which all referred to this witness. That's all we've had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is something that I have seen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that is not satisfactory. I know that Mr. Cunningham has been absent. Mr. Cunningham, the case manager, and Mr. Ackerman now. What we're asking for is an order of compliance with the rule, and that is there should be a list of exhibits for the defence Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. case. As I said when we had the pre-Defence conference, obviously there will be occasions when witnesses arrive unexpectedly with extra documents. Your Honour, the documents that were produced through this witness, which we've got urgent translations of last night, might have been anticipated, because it's clear from the summary that this witness was going to refer to them. Those documents should have been obtained by the Defence. It doesn't require a massive amount of efficiency to do so- well in advance, should have been on the advance witness list, copies should have been supplied to us in advance, whether translated or not. Because this can't have been unexpected documents. It's not like a witness arriving with a diary or the like. So, Your Honour, all together, we do say this is not satisfactory and would like Your Honours to make an order that we receive a proper, full exhibit list, plus copies of documents that it is known that the witnesses will be dealing with. That's the first point that I make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the second point that I make is this: Witness number 2 on the list, and I'll refer to him by the number, was due to come next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the original --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the original list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I take it that next week you're going to have the military expert here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The reason being that we were informed that witness number 2 couldn't come. The only reason I'm raising that is this: Your Honour, this is a major, major, major witness. Your Honours have already discussed with us, I think, that he's likely to take a very long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine, say two days is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We have a quantity, I mean really a quantity of information about him, and therefore, we would like proper advance notice of this particular witness when he comes again. In other words, what I'm asking is that he's not suddenly put in. We do need sufficient notice for him, and any other member of the Crisis Staff who is going to give evidence. Your Honour, the third matter is for us, we hope the Prosecutor has not been here, but we drafted a cleaned up indictment if I can put it that way should be lodged sometime next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no hurry for that because actually my inclination was, Ms. Korner, to ask you to defer that to after we have handed down the written decision on the Rule 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
